state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let me ask you this: what would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, okay... so like, if I had simpler numbers, maybe 10 and 20? So the range would be 10. Then if they all grew by 3 cm, they'd be 13 and 23, so the range would still be 10... but wait, if I cut them in half they'd be 5 and 10, and that's still a range of 5, not 10. So maybe I got it backwards?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What do you think this tells us about the relationship between changing all values by the same proportion and the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so like... if you add the same amount to everything, the range stays the same, but if you multiply everything by the same number, the range changes too? So Katie was actually right and Tom was wrong? I'm still a bit confused about why adding doesn't change it but multiplying does though.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively uses a simple example to help the student discover their misconception about proportional changes, leading to clear improvement from believing 'Only Tom' to correctly identifying Katie, though the student still seeks deeper understanding at the end.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher perfectly exemplifies the Socratic method by using only probing questions that guide the student to discover their own error through a simpler counterexample, never directly stating the answer or explanation.
